BREAST__Breast Cancer:
Overview — The Breast Cancer Framework
The commonest cancer in women. The framework: triple assessment to diagnose, receptor status (ER/PR/HER2) to treat, and TNM + NPI to prognosticate.
The three questions that drive everything: Is it cancer? (triple assessment) → What type + receptors? (histology) → How far + how aggressive? (staging / grade).
Cross-ref: benign breast disease (the differential cluster), screening / 2WW (next tab), and axillary surgery complications (lymphoedema).
Risk Factors — Mostly Oestrogen Exposure + Genetics
📷 Image placeholder — Male breast cancer — rare but high-yield: strong BRCA2 and Klinefelter's association; presents as a firm subareolar lump, managed on the same triple-assessment/receptor pathway.
Genetic
  • BRCA1 / BRCA2 — the key inherited cause
↑ Oestrogen exposure
  • Nulliparity, late first pregnancy
  • Early menarche, late menopause
  • COCP / HRT
  • Obesity (peripheral oestrogen)
Other
  • Increasing age
  • Prior breast cancer
  • Family history
Pathological Types
  • Invasive ductal carcinoma (NST — no special type) = commonest
  • Invasive lobular carcinoma
  • DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ) — pre-invasive; classic feature = comedo necrosis; seen as microcalcification on mammogram
  • LCIS (lobular carcinoma in situ)
  • Inflammatory breast cancer — progressive erythema + oedema (peau d'orange) without infection; aggressive, the key mimic of mastitis
  • Paget's disease of the nipple — nipple eczema/reddening → underlying malignancy
Receptor Status — Drives Treatment
ReceptorSignificanceTargeted treatment
ER / PR (hormone)Hormone-driven growthEndocrine therapy (tamoxifen / anastrozole)
HER2Growth-factor receptor, aggressiveTrastuzumab (Herceptin)
Triple-negative (all −)Worse prognosis — limits targeted optionsChemo-reliant
Presentation
  • Hard, irregular lump, ± nipple inversion or skin tethering
  • Skin changes (peau d'orange, ulceration), nipple discharge (esp. bloody), axillary lump
Metastasis sites — "2 Ls and 2 Bs": Lungs, Liver, Bones, Brain. Any metastatic tumour could have a breast primary.
Triple Assessment — The Diagnostic Framework
Every suspicious breast lump gets all three components.
ComponentTest
1. ClinicalHistory + examination
2. ImagingUSS (<40 / dense breasts); mammogram (>40)
3. PathologyCore biopsy (preferred — gives histology + receptors) ± FNA cytology
Radiological clues: spiculated mass, microcalcification (esp. DCIS), architectural distortion.
Staging & Prognosis
  • TNM (tumour, nodes, metastasis); all patients discussed at MDT
  • Gene-expression profiling (NICE DG34) for early ER+/HER2−/node− cancers → predicts recurrence risk + guides whether to add chemo
  • Nottingham Prognostic Index (NPI) — combines tumour size, nodal status and histological grade into good/moderate/poor groups
  • Grade: Scarff-Bloom-Richardson (tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses)
Treatment — Surgery → Adjuvant by Receptor/Node Status
Surgery (first-line)
  • Tumour <4 cm → wide local excision (WLE); larger/multifocal → mastectomy (± reconstruction)
  • Axilla: palpable nodes → axillary node clearance; impalpable → pre-op axillary USS ± biopsy: if positive → axillary node clearance; if negative → sentinel node biopsy
  • Axillary clearance risks arm lymphoedema + functional impairment
Radiotherapy: whole-breast radiotherapy for ALL women after wide local excision.
Endocrine therapy (ER+)
SettingDrugMechanismKey SE
Pre-menopausalTamoxifenSERM (partial ER antagonist)Hot flushes, menstrual changes, VTE, endometrial cancer risk
Post-menopausalAnastrozoleAromatase inhibitor (blocks peripheral oestrogen)Osteoporosis
  • HER2+: adjuvant trastuzumab (Herceptin) — cardiotoxic, monitor LV function
  • Chemotherapy: FEC-D if node-positive; FEC if node-negative; neoadjuvant to downstage large tumours
  • Metastatic/palliative: systemic therapy by receptor, bone-directed treatment, symptom control, MDT + supportive care (rehab, nurse counsellors, palliative input)

Triple assessment
Clinical + imaging (USS <40 / mammogram >40) + core biopsy for every suspicious lump.

IDC (NST) commonest; DCIS → comedo necrosis + microcalcification; inflammatory = peau d'orange, mimics mastitis.

ER+ → tamoxifen (pre) / anastrozole (post); HER2+ → trastuzumab; triple-negative = worst prognosis.

Tamoxifen → VTE + endometrial cancer (SERM); anastrozole → osteoporosis (aromatase inhibitor).

<4 cm → WLE + whole-breast radiotherapy (WLE always gets radiotherapy).
Axilla
Palpable → clearance (→ lymphoedema); impalpable → USS → sentinel node biopsy.
Chemo

Mets = 2 Ls + 2 Bs

Screening Programme
📷 Image placeholder — NHSBSP screening — 3-yearly mammography, ages 50–70 (AgeX trial evaluating extension to 47–73).
Mammogram every 3 years for women aged 50–70 — the NHS Breast Screening Programme.

  • Trade-offs: catches early disease but with overdiagnosis / false-positive costs
  • High-risk (e.g. BRCA): earlier + MRI-based surveillance

Overview — Triage & Triple Assessment
A differential cluster covering the non-cancerous causes of breast lumps, pain, nipple discharge and skin change. The skill examined is placing a breast symptom in the right box while always excluding cancer first — which is why triple assessment is the spine of the whole cluster, not any individual diagnosis.
The decisive first split is what is the presenting symptom — lump, pain, discharge or skin change — because each opens onto a different short differential and a different "cancer mimic" you must not miss. Cross-ref the Breast Cancer note (any suspicious finding routes to the 2WW pathway).
The Triage Table
PresentationBenign causesMalignancy to exclude
Discrete lumpFibroadenoma (young, mobile), cyst (perimenopausal), fat necrosis (post-trauma)Carcinoma
Lumpy + painful, cyclicalFibrocystic change—
Nipple dischargeDuct ectasia (green-brown, multi-duct), intraductal papilloma (bloody, single-duct)Carcinoma (bloody discharge)
Nipple skin changeEczema (starts at areola)Paget's disease (starts at nipple)
Erythema, tender, swollenMastitis / abscessInflammatory breast cancer
Three can't-miss mimics: fat necrosis (mimics a carcinomatous lump), Paget's (mimics eczema), inflammatory cancer (mimics mastitis). Every benign diagnosis here is one of exclusion via triple assessment.
Triple Assessment — The Central Framework
📷 Image placeholder — Triple assessment — clinical examination + imaging (USS/mammography) + core biopsy, each scored; concordance gives a safe benign diagnosis, discordance mandates further investigation.
Combines clinical examination, imaging and biopsy for all women with a discrete palpable mass. Each component is scored, and concordance of the three gives confidence in a benign diagnosis — a discordant result mandates further investigation.
ComponentInvolvesNotes
1. ClinicalHistory + breast & axillary examinationAge + risk factors shape pre-test probability
2. ImagingUSS if <40 / dense breasts; mammography if >40USS better in dense young tissue; mammography detects microcalcification
3. PathologyCore biopsy (preferred — histology + receptors) ± FNA cytologyCore biopsy distinguishes invasive from in-situ disease
In women under 30, breast nodularity may be managed with clinical surveillance + short-term re-examination in 2–3 months rather than immediate biopsy, reflecting the lower cancer risk.
The Nipple Discharge Discriminator
📷 Image placeholder — Two-branch decision diagram — single-duct + bloody (± retroareolar nodule) → intraductal papilloma; multi-duct + green/brown → duct ectasia; any bloody discharge → investigate to exclude carcinoma.
Two questions resolve most nipple discharge: how many ducts, and is it bloody. A single duct + bloody discharge (± small retroareolar nodule) → intraductal papilloma; multi-duct + green/yellow/clear → duct ectasia. Any bloody discharge must be investigated to exclude carcinoma, even though the commonest cause (papilloma) is benign.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Every discrete lump → triple assessment
Clinical + imaging (USS <40/dense, mammogram >40) + core biopsy.
Diagnosis rests on concordance
Discordance → further investigation, however benign one component looks.
Three cancer mimics
Fat necrosis (lump), Paget's (nipple skin), inflammatory cancer (red tender breast).
Nipple discharge
Single-duct bloody → papilloma; multi-duct green-brown → duct ectasia; bloody always excludes cancer.
Under 30 + nodularity
Short-interval clinical surveillance is reasonable before biopsy.
Overview
The commonest benign breast tumour in young women, typically 15–35. Localised proliferation of breast ducts and stroma, developing from a whole lobule — an "aberration of normal development" rather than a true neoplasm.
  • No meaningful increase in breast cancer risk
  • A significant proportion regress spontaneously over a few years
Clinical Features
  • A highly mobile, firm, smooth, well-defined, non-tender lump — so mobile it's nicknamed the "breast mouse" (slips away under the fingers)
  • Typically oval with well-defined margins; often multiple (simultaneously or sequentially)
Investigations
  • Triple assessment, as for any lump. On USS: a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesion with benign features
  • Core biopsy confirms the diagnosis — and biopsy confirmation removes the need for serial USS follow-up
Giant fibroadenoma (>5 cm) and the related phyllodes tumour (can be borderline/malignant, recurs locally) are the differentials for a large or rapidly growing lesion — don't assume benign without histology.
Management
  • Conservative is the default — reassurance + discharge (benign, tends to regress)
  • Surgical excision if >3 cm, enlarging, significantly symptomatic, or patient preference
⭐ Exam Pearls
Young woman + mobile, firm, smooth, painless lump
= fibroadenoma ("breast mouse").
No increased cancer risk
Many regress; biopsy confirmation removes the need for serial USS.
Conservative
Excise if >3 cm / enlarging / symptomatic.
Large or rapidly growing
Consider phyllodes tumour → excise for histology.
Overview
Fluid-filled, epithelium-lined sacs — a common cause of a discrete lump in the perimenopausal years (~35–50). Hormonally driven, part of the fibrocystic spectrum.
  • Simple cysts carry no increased breast cancer risk
  • Caveat: a complex cyst (solid components / thick septations) warrants further assessment
Clinical Features
  • A smooth, mobile, sometimes tender lump; rubbery, often multiple
  • Can appear suddenly and fluctuate with the menstrual cycle; a tense cyst can be painful
Investigations
  • Triple assessment. USS: a simple cyst is anechoic (clean black fluid) with posterior acoustic enhancement — usually diagnostic
  • Mammography: a cyst can produce the characteristic radiolucent "halo sign"
A complex cyst (internal echoes, solid mural components) needs biopsy/aspiration cytology to exclude malignancy.
Management
  • Asymptomatic simple cysts — no treatment
  • Symptomatic → aspiration (diagnostic + therapeutic)
Two findings at aspiration trigger further investigation to exclude carcinoma: bloodstained aspirate, or a residual mass after aspiration → imaging + biopsy.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Perimenopausal + smooth mobile lump
= breast cyst; often multiple, fluctuate with the cycle.
Imaging
USS = anechoic; mammogram = halo sign.
Aspirate if symptomatic
Diagnostic + therapeutic.
Red flags at aspiration
Bloodstained aspirate or residual mass → investigate for malignancy.
Simple = no cancer risk
Complex cyst → biopsy.
Overview
A benign, hormonally-driven condition: the breast becomes lumpy, nodular and often painful, fluctuating across the menstrual cycle. An exaggerated physiological response to cyclical hormones rather than a disease — hence much management is reassurance.
  • Middle reproductive years (~30–50); sits on the same spectrum as breast cysts (often coexist)
  • No increased breast cancer risk in its common (non-proliferative) form
Clinical Features
  • Lumpy, nodular breasts — often bilateral & diffuse rather than a single mass — with pain worse pre-menstrually, easing after menstruation
  • The nodularity is what brings the patient in → diagnose by triple assessment to exclude a discrete malignant lump, then reassure
Mastalgia
First step: distinguish true breast pain from chest-wall pain (costochondritis, musculoskeletal).
CyclicalNon-cyclical
TimingWorse pre-menstrually, eases after periodUnrelated to cycle
MechanismHormonal (fibrocystic)Duct ectasia, large pendulous breasts, referred chest-wall pain
LateralityUsually bilateral, diffuseOften focal / unilateral
Management of mastalgia: reassurance (most resolves), a well-fitted supportive bra, simple analgesia / topical NSAIDs. Severe refractory cyclical pain has specialist options (danazol, tamoxifen) — rarely needed at student level.
Investigations
  • Triple assessment if there is a discrete or dominant lump within the nodularity
  • If imaging shows only diffuse fibrocystic change with no discrete lesion → reassure
⭐ Exam Pearls
Lumpy, tender breasts worse before periods
= fibrocystic change; middle reproductive years; no increased cancer risk (common form).
Cyclical mastalgia
Hormonal, bilateral, pre-menstrual → reassurance + supportive bra + simple/topical analgesia.
Distinguish breast vs chest-wall pain first
A discrete dominant lump
Still needs triple assessment — don't attribute every lump to fibrocystic change.
Overview
Benign dilation + inflammation of the large central (sub-areolar) ducts, producing nipple discharge and sometimes retraction ("ectasia" = dilation). Ducts dilate and shorten with age (within ~3 cm of the nipple).
  • Classically perimenopausal / menopausal women; commoner in overweight women; associated with prior lactation
  • Significant overlap with periductal mastitis — often the same process
Clinical Features
  • Green, brown or creamy discharge, characteristically from multiple ducts — colour + multi-duct nature are the key benign signals (vs single-duct bloody papilloma)
  • Nipple retraction/inversion (periductal fibrosis) ± small sub-areolar lump — the retraction is what raises cancer concern
  • Smoking is a recognised risk factor (stronger for the periductal-mastitis end)
Investigations
  • Triple assessment, principally to exclude carcinoma — nipple retraction + discharge are also red flags for malignancy
  • Mammogram/USS; ductal assessment where discharge is bloody or single-duct
Management
  • No specific treatment if mild — reassurance once cancer excluded
  • Troublesome → surgical duct excision: microdochectomy (single-duct, preferred in younger women wishing to breastfeed) or total duct excision (older / multi-duct)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Perimenopausal + green-brown, multi-duct discharge ± retraction
= duct ectasia.
Benign mimic of cancer's nipple changes
Triple-assess to exclude malignancy (retraction is a shared red flag).
Smoking-associated
Overlaps with periductal mastitis.
Surgery if needed
Microdochectomy (young, single duct) vs total duct excision (older, multi-duct).
Overview
A benign warty tumour growing within a lactiferous (milk) duct, typically sub-areolar. Classic presentation: a single duct + bloody, sudden discharge ± small retroareolar nodule. Most commonly 35–55.
Benign — but because it presents with bloody nipple discharge (also cardinal for malignancy), it can never be assumed benign without investigation.
Clinical Features
  • Bloodstained (or clear/serous) discharge from a single duct — the hallmark and the key discriminator from duct ectasia's multi-duct green-brown discharge
  • Usually no palpable lump, unless large enough to form a small retroareolar nodule
Investigations
  • Triple assessment. Single-duct bloody discharge warrants ductal imaging (USS, ± ductography/ductoscopy) alongside mammography
  • Core/excision biopsy — a single-duct papilloma must be distinguished from DCIS, and atypia within a papilloma carries some malignant potential
Management
Microdochectomy — excision of the affected duct — is both diagnostic (histology to exclude malignancy) and therapeutic (resolves the discharge).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Single-duct, bloodstained discharge ± small/no nodule
= intraductal papilloma.
Benign cause of bloody discharge
But always excised (microdochectomy) to exclude carcinoma/DCIS.
The clean discriminator
Papilloma = single-duct, bloody; duct ectasia = multi-duct, green-brown.
Overview
Benign inflammatory process — damaged adipose tissue undergoes necrosis + fibrosis, producing a firm lump. Its whole importance: it is the classic benign mimic of carcinoma — a hard, irregular, fixed lump (± skin tethering) clinically and radiologically indistinguishable from cancer.
  • Typically obese women with large, pendulous breasts
  • Characteristically follows trauma — often trivial or unremembered (seatbelt, a knock, prior surgery/radiotherapy)
Clinical Features
  • Initially a firm, round lump; over time may organise into a hard, irregular, fixed lump ± skin tethering/dimpling — the features that mimic malignancy (usually painless)
  • A history of trauma/surgery supports it — but its absence doesn't exclude it
Investigations
Triple assessment is mandatory — you cannot distinguish fat necrosis from carcinoma clinically. Imaging may itself show suspicious features (spiculated mass, calcification), so core biopsy is critical to obtain histology and exclude malignancy.
Management
  • Once malignancy is confidently excluded on biopsy → conservative (typically resolves over time)
  • Excision only if it remains symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain
⭐ Exam Pearls
Obese, large breasts, preceding (often trivial/forgotten) trauma
→ hard, irregular lump that mimics cancer.
The benign lump you must triple-assess
Indistinguishable from carcinoma — biopsy is what makes the diagnosis safe.
Conservative once cancer excluded
Resolves spontaneously.
Overview
Mastitis = inflammation of breast tissue ± infection; untreated/inadequately treated bacterial mastitis can progress to a breast abscess (walled-off pus). The decisive fork is lactational vs periductal (non-lactational) — different patients, organisms and antibiotics.
The Two Types
LactationalPeriductal (non-lactational)
ContextBreastfeeding women; milk stasis the triggerSmokers; assoc. duct ectasia; recurrent
OrganismStaph aureus via cracked nippleMixed flora (anaerobes/staph)
PresentationPainful, tender, erythematous, swollen breast (often segmental) ± systemic upsetPeri-areolar inflammation ± abscess ± mammary duct fistula
First-lineContinue breastfeeding / milk removal — stopping worsens stasisCo-amoxiclav
Lactational Mastitis — Management
  • First-line = continued breastfeeding + effective milk removal — counterintuitive but essential, as stopping causes milk stasis → abscess
  • Antibiotics (flucloxacillin, 10–14 days) added if systemically unwell, a nipple fissure, or no improvement after 12–24 h of effective milk removal
Breast Abscess
  • Suspect with a fluctuant, tender mass + overlying erythema, persistent fever, or antibiotic failure
  • Management = drainage — USS-guided needle aspiration (often first-line for smaller abscesses) or incision & drainage, plus antibiotics
Can't-miss mimic: inflammatory breast cancer — red, swollen, oedematous breast (peau d'orange) without infection features and not responding to antibiotics. Any "mastitis" that doesn't settle must be investigated to exclude it.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Lactational = milk stasis + Staph aureus
Keep breastfeeding + flucloxacillin if unwell/fissure/no improvement in 12–24 h. Don't stop feeding (causes abscess).
Periductal = smokers + duct ectasia
Co-amoxiclav.
Abscess → drainage
USS-guided aspiration or I&D + antibiotics.
Non-resolving "mastitis"
Exclude inflammatory breast cancer.
Overview
An eczema-like change of the nipple that signals underlying breast malignancy — it looks benign but is associated with an underlying DCIS or invasive cancer in the great majority. Histologically: malignant (Paget) cells within the nipple epidermis.
A red flag masquerading as a benign nipple complaint — the trap is to treat it as eczema and miss the cancer.
Clinical Features & the Key Discriminator
📷 Image placeholder — Paget's vs nipple eczema — Paget's begins at the NIPPLE and spreads outward to the areola, whereas eczema begins at the areola and spares the nipple.
  • Reddening, thickening and scaling that begins at the NIPPLE and spreads to the areola, ± itching, ulceration or discharge
The classic discriminator (single most-tested point): Paget's starts at the nipple and spreads to the areola; nipple eczema starts at the areola and spares the nipple. A persistent unilateral nipple change is Paget's until proven otherwise.
Investigations
  • Biopsy of the nipple skin to confirm Paget cells
  • Mammography/USS to identify the underlying malignancy (DCIS or invasive), which co-exists in most cases — triple assessment principles apply
Management
  • Directed at the underlying breast cancer — surgery (mastectomy, or breast-conserving surgery with nipple excision depending on the disease) + appropriate adjuvant therapy (cross-ref Breast Cancer note)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Unilateral eczematous change that STARTS AT THE NIPPLE
= Paget's (vs eczema, which starts at the areola and spares the nipple).
Almost always overlies DCIS or invasive cancer
Biopsy + imaging to find the underlying malignancy.
Manage the underlying cancer
Never dismiss a persistent nipple change as simple eczema.
BREAST__Triple Assessment & Imaging:
Triple assessment is the standard "one-stop" work-up for a breast lump or any suspicious breast symptom. It combines three independent arms — clinical (history + examination), imaging (radiology), and pathology (tissue/cytology). Each arm is scored 1–5 for rising suspicion of malignancy, and combining them maximises diagnostic accuracy: a cancer missed by one modality is usually caught by another. Suspicious symptoms trigger an urgent 2-week-wait referral to a breast clinic, where all three arms are performed at a single visit. See Breast cancer ›.
1The three arms — each scored 1–5
The heart of triple assessment is that three separate modalities each independently rate the lesion on the same 1–5 scale: 1 = normal, 2 = benign, 3 = uncertain / probably benign, 4 = suspicious, 5 = malignant. The prefix letter tells you which arm produced the score.
🩺Clinical — P1–P5
History + examination. P = palpation. P1 normal → P5 malignant.
📷Imaging — M/U 1–5
M = mammogram, U = ultrasound (often written R1–R5). M/U1 normal → M/U5 malignant.
🔬Pathology — B/C 1–5
B = core biopsy (preferred — gives histology + receptor status), C = FNA cytology. B/C1 normal → B/C5 malignant.
1 normal2 benign3 uncertain4 suspicious5 malignant
Core biopsy (B) is preferred over FNA (C) because it distinguishes invasive from in-situ disease and provides ER/PR/HER2 status to guide treatment.
2Imaging choice depends on age
The imaging modality is chosen by patient age because young, dense breast tissue is poorly seen on mammography.
Age <40 or dense breasts→Ultrasound (U) — better in dense tissue
Age ≥40 / screening→Mammography (M) ± ultrasound
In practice both are often used together in older patients; ultrasound also guides the biopsy needle in real time.
3Concordance — the arms must agree
The three arms should give concordant (agreeing) results. When they do, you can act on them with confidence. When they disagree (discordance) — for example a benign biopsy but suspicious imaging or examination — further assessment is mandatory.
  • Concordant benign (e.g. P2/U2/B2) → reassure and discharge or routine follow-up.
  • Concordant malignant (e.g. P5/M5/B5) → MDT and definitive cancer management.
  • Discordant (any suspicious arm not confirmed) → repeat biopsy or diagnostic excision; never rely on one reassuring result.
A single benign component does not override clinical or radiological suspicion — it is the combination that is safe, not any one arm alone.
🚩
Discordant results must trigger further assessment. A benign biopsy that conflicts with a suspicious examination or scan is not reassuring — arrange repeat core biopsy or excision. A single benign arm never overrules suspicion. Refer via urgent 2-week-wait if: new discrete lump (especially age >30), unilateral bloody nipple discharge, skin or nipple change (retraction, tethering, peau d’orange, eczema of the nipple), or an axillary lump.
📷 Image placeholder — a three-column flow diagram: "Clinical (P1–5)", "Imaging (M/U1–5)", "Pathology (B/C1–5)" feeding into a central box "Concordance?" with two exits: "Agree → act" and "Discordant → further assessment / excision".
🎓 Exam pearl. Remember the letters: P (palpation/clinical), M/U (mammogram/ultrasound), B/C (biopsy/cytology) — all scored 1–5. Favourite finals traps: choose ultrasound in the under-40s; prefer core biopsy over FNA (histology + receptors); and discordance always wins — a benign biopsy never cancels a suspicious lump.
Breast ultrasound (USS) is the first-line breast imaging in women under 40 and in those with dense breasts, because young, radiodense glandular tissue lowers mammographic sensitivity — dense tissue and cancer both appear white, masking lesions. USS uses no ionising radiation, so it is also preferred in pregnancy and lactation. It is a core part of triple assessment.
1Why USS first under 40 / in dense breasts
In young or dense breasts the glandular tissue is radiodense, so mammography loses sensitivity — both normal dense tissue and tumour appear white, hiding masses. USS is superior in this group and carries no radiation, making it the imaging of choice under 40 and in pregnancy/lactation.
📡USS (<40 / dense)
First-line; no radiation; solid vs cystic; safe in pregnancy.
🩻Mammography (≥40)
Primary imaging ≥40 & screening; best for microcalcification / DCIS.
2What USS is used for
  • Distinguishes solid from cystic lesions.
  • Characterises masses (benign vs suspicious features).
  • Guides needle procedures — USS-guided core biopsy/FNA and cyst aspiration.
  • Assesses the axilla for abnormal nodes, with node biopsy if indicated.
Solid vs cysticImage-guided biopsyAxillary staging
3Benign vs suspicious features
Benign — well-defined, smooth/oval, wider-than-tall (parallel to skin), hypoechoic, thin capsule (e.g. fibroadenoma). A simple cyst is anechoic with posterior acoustic enhancement and thin walls.
Wider-than-tall, smooth, capsule→Likely benign (fibroadenoma)
Taller-than-wide, irregular, spiculated→Suspicious — posterior shadowing, microcalcification, abnormal nodes
See also Benign breast disease ›
4Complementary role & scoring
In women ≥40 or for screening, mammography is the primary imaging (better for microcalcification/DCIS), often combined with USS. USS is part of triple assessment and is scored U1–U5 (U1 normal → U5 malignant).
Triple assessment = clinical exam + imaging (USS ± mammography) + histology/cytology.
🚩
A normal or benign USS does NOT exclude cancer if clinical or other suspicion persists — complete full triple assessment and biopsy. Do not rely on USS alone for microcalcification/DCIS, where mammography is needed.
📷 Image placeholder — side-by-side USS: a benign fibroadenoma (well-defined, oval, wider-than-tall, hypoechoic) versus a suspicious carcinoma (irregular, taller-than-wide, spiculated with posterior acoustic shadowing).
🎓 Exam pearl. Under 40 or dense breasts (and pregnancy) → USS first, no radiation. Benign = wider-than-tall with posterior enhancement; malignant = taller-than-wide with posterior shadowing. USS is scored U1–U5 within triple assessment, and a reassuring scan never overrides ongoing clinical concern.
Mammography is low-dose X-ray breast imaging and the primary imaging modality in women ≥40 and the basis of the NHS Breast Screening Programme. Two standard views are taken per breast — craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO). It is uniquely good at detecting microcalcification and therefore DCIS, which ultrasound often misses. Sensitivity is highest in older, fattier (less dense) breasts and falls in dense/young breasts — where USS is preferred. See Breast cancer ›.
1Views, indications & NHS screening
Every mammogram is two views per breast: CC and MLO. It is the first-line image in symptomatic patients ≥40 (usually alongside USS) and the tool of the national screening programme.
CC viewMLO view≥40 primary imaging
NHS Breast Screening→women 50–70 (extending 47–73) invited every 3 years
Screening detects→impalpable cancers, especially DCIS via microcalcification
Under 40 or in pregnancy, use USS first-line (denser breast tissue, avoid radiation dose).
2Malignant vs benign features
The hallmark of malignancy is clustered / pleomorphic microcalcification (DCIS). Mammography is the modality uniquely able to detect it — USS commonly misses microcalcification.
🩻Malignant features
Clustered/pleomorphic microcalcification, spiculated/irregular mass, architectural distortion, focal asymmetry, skin/nipple changes.
🩻Benign features
Well-defined round/oval mass, coarse "popcorn" calcification (involuting fibroadenoma), rim/eggshell calcification (cyst/fat necrosis), lucent fatty lesions.
3Scoring & role in triple assessment
Mammograms are scored M1–M5 as part of triple assessment (clinical exam + imaging + biopsy).
  • M1 normal → M5 malignant.
  • Diagnostic mammography in symptomatic patients ≥40, usually with USS.
  • Stereotactic / mammographic guidance is used to biopsy microcalcification not visible on USS.
Involves a small radiation dose — avoid as first-line under 40 or in pregnancy.
🚩
A normal mammogram does NOT exclude cancer in a symptomatic or dense (young) breast — sensitivity is reduced in dense tissue. If a lump is clinically suspicious, complete triple assessment with USS ± biopsy regardless of the mammogram. Use USS not mammography as first-line under 40.
📷 Image placeholder — CC and MLO mammographic views of one breast showing a cluster of fine pleomorphic microcalcifications in the upper outer quadrant (magnified inset), typical of high-grade DCIS.
🎓 Exam pearl. Two views per breast = CC + MLO. Mammography is primary imaging ≥40 and uniquely detects microcalcification/DCIS that USS misses; the NHS screens 50–70 every 3 years. But a normal mammogram never excludes cancer in a suspicious lump or dense breast — always finish triple assessment, and use USS first under 40.
Ductography (galactography) is a contrast study of a single breast duct. A fine cannula is passed into the discharging duct orifice, iodinated contrast is injected, and mammography outlines the duct to reveal an intraductal filling defect or duct cut-off. It is used to investigate pathological single-duct, spontaneous, bloody (or serous/clear) nipple discharge from one duct — where the classic cause is an intraductal papilloma, but DCIS / carcinoma must be excluded.
1What ductography shows
The cannulated duct is opacified with contrast and imaged on mammography. The study localises the lesion and looks for an intraductal filling defect or an abrupt duct cut-off / obstruction.
Smooth filling defect / duct dilatation→Intraductal papilloma (commonest cause)
Irregular defect / duct cut-off→Suspicious — exclude DCIS / carcinoma
Dilated, tortuous subareolar ducts→Duct ectasia
2Key differential of single-duct bloody discharge
🩸Intraductal papilloma
Commonest cause — benign, but the classic cause of bloody single-duct discharge.
🟡Duct ectasia
Dilated subareolar ducts; usually green/creamy but can be blood-stained.
⚠️DCIS / carcinoma
The important one to exclude — underlying malignancy must be ruled out.
3Where it fits in modern practice
Pathological discharge is assessed within triple assessment — clinical exam, imaging (USS ± mammography) and pathology. Test the discharge for blood; discharge cytology is of limited value.
USS / mammographyMRIDuctoscopyMicrodochectomy
  • Microdochectomy (single-duct excision) or total duct excision is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
  • MRI and direct ductoscopy are increasingly used; ductography is now less commonly performed but remains a classic exam topic.
Milky bilateral discharge (galactorrhoea) → check prolactin and drug history rather than image a single duct.
🚩
Worrying nipple discharge: unilateral, single-duct, spontaneous, blood-stained, associated mass, or age >50 → 2-week-wait referral for triple assessment. Reassuring: bilateral, multi-duct, only on expression, milky (galactorrhoea) or green/creamy (duct ectasia). Microdochectomy is diagnostic and therapeutic — always exclude Breast cancer ›.
📷 Image placeholder — ductogram: a single subareolar duct opacified with contrast, showing a rounded intraductal filling defect (papilloma) with proximal duct dilatation and distal duct cut-off.
🎓 Exam pearl. Ductography images one discharging duct to find a filling defect. Single-duct bloody discharge is classically an intraductal papilloma, but you must exclude DCIS / carcinoma. Remember the worrying triad — unilateral, single-duct, spontaneous, bloody — and that microdochectomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
BREAST__Pathology & Staging:
Once the triple assessment finds a suspicious lump, the diagnosis is nailed down by core needle biopsy — the preferred pathology arm. A wide-bore needle (USS- or stereotactically guided) removes an actual tissue core, giving histology rather than the loose cells of FNA cytology. This single sample tells you whether the cancer is invasive or in situ (DCIS), its grade, and — via immunohistochemistry — its ER, PR and HER2 receptor status, which directs the whole treatment plan.
1Core biopsy vs FNA — why the core wins
FNA cytology only tells you if cells look malignant. A core biopsy preserves tissue architecture, so it can do far more:
  • Distinguishes invasive carcinoma from in situ disease (DCIS) — FNA cannot.
  • Provides tumour grade and tissue for ER/PR/HER2 receptor testing.
  • Allows assessment before neoadjuvant therapy and placement of a marker clip.
Wide-bore needleImage-guided (USS / stereotactic)Gives histology
2The B1–B5 histology score
Breast core biopsies are reported on a standardised B (biopsy) category:
B1→Normal / uninformative
B2→Benign (e.g. fibroadenoma)
B3→Uncertain malignant potential / atypia — needs excision
B4→Suspicious of malignancy
B5a→Malignant, in situ (DCIS)
B5b→Malignant, invasive
A B3 result — atypical ductal hyperplasia, a papillary lesion or radial scar — usually needs diagnostic vacuum-assisted or surgical excision because occult malignancy may be present.
3Receptor status (ER / PR / HER2) directs treatment
Receptor status is assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) on the core and is both prognostic and predictive:
🟢ER / PR positive
Hormone-receptor positive → responds to endocrine therapy: tamoxifen (pre-menopausal) or an aromatase inhibitor (post-menopausal). Good prognostic marker.
🎯HER2 positive
Over-expressed / amplified → more aggressive but responds to anti-HER2 targeted therapy: trastuzumab (Herceptin) ± pertuzumab. IHC 3+ positive; equivocal 2+ reflexed to ISH/FISH.
⚠️Triple-negative
ER−, PR−, HER2− — no endocrine or anti-HER2 target, poorer prognosis. Treated with chemotherapy (± immunotherapy); associated with BRCA1.
🚩
Always ensure receptor status (ER/PR/HER2) is obtained — it changes management (ER+ → endocrine therapy; HER2+ → trastuzumab; triple-negative → chemotherapy). A B3 / atypical result, or any biopsy result that is discordant with the imaging or clinical picture, must be escalated for diagnostic excision or vacuum-assisted biopsy — never accept a benign core if the lesion looks malignant.
📷 Image placeholder — ultrasound-guided core biopsy in progress: a spring-loaded wide-bore needle within a hypoechoic irregular mass, alongside an H&E histology slide showing invasive ductal carcinoma and a brown-stained ER-positive IHC panel.
🎓 Exam pearl. The classic OSCE distinction: FNA = cytology (cells only), core biopsy = histology (invasive vs in situ, grade, and receptor status). Remember ER+ → tamoxifen / aromatase inhibitor, HER2+ → trastuzumab, and triple-negative → chemotherapy + think BRCA1. Histology is graded B1–B5 (B5a in situ, B5b invasive), and a B3 always earns a further excision. Breast cancer ›
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) cytology uses a fine needle to aspirate individual cells (not a tissue core) from a breast lump or lymph node for cytological examination. It is quick, cheap and minimally invasive, and results are reported on a C1–C5 scale. Because it samples cells rather than architecture, core biopsy has largely replaced FNA as the primary pathology arm of triple assessment — but FNA still has valuable niches. See Breast cancer ›
1What it is & how it’s reported (C1–C5)
A fine needle (often under ultrasound guidance) aspirates cells directly onto slides for the cytologist. It is a component of triple assessment (clinical exam + imaging + pathology). Reporting uses the C-category system:
C1 inadequate/acellularC2 benignC3 atypia, probably benignC4 suspiciousC5 malignant
A C1 result means the sample is non-diagnostic and must be repeated — FNA has a higher inadequate rate than core biopsy and is operator-dependent.
2Why core biopsy has largely replaced it
FNA gives cytology only — loose individual cells with no tissue architecture. This creates two decisive limitations for cancer work-up:
  • It cannot distinguish invasive cancer from in-situ disease (DCIS) — that distinction needs the tissue architecture only a core biopsy provides.
  • It does not reliably give receptor status (ER / PR / HER2), which is essential to plan systemic treatment.
  • Higher inadequate (C1) rate and greater operator dependence.
Need invasive vs in-situ + ER/PR/HER2→Core biopsy, not FNA
3Where FNA is still useful
FNA retains a clear role where cells alone answer the question or drainage is therapeutic:
💉Cyst aspiration
Confirms and drains a symptomatic simple cyst. Non-bloody fluid + lump disappears = benign; cytology not needed.
🎯Axillary node staging
FNA (or core) of a suspicious axillary lymph node seen on USS to stage the axilla pre-operatively.
⚡Rapid recurrence check
Quick confirmation of obvious recurrence or sampling of clearly benign lesions.
🚩
Cyst aspiration rule. Clear / straw / green fluid with the lump fully resolving → reassure, no cytology. But send fluid and proceed to imaging + biopsy if the fluid is bloodstained, a residual mass remains, or the cyst recurs — to exclude an intracystic carcinoma.
📷 Image placeholder — ultrasound-guided FNA of a breast lump with a cytology slide alongside, showing dispersed epithelial cells (no tissue architecture) contrasted with a core-biopsy specimen showing intact ducts and stroma.
🎓 Exam pearl. FNA = cells (C1–C5); core biopsy = tissue (B1–B5). If a stem asks why core biopsy is preferred, the answer is that FNA cannot separate invasive from in-situ (DCIS) and cannot give ER/PR/HER2. Remember FNA still shines for cyst aspiration and axillary node sampling — and bloodstained cyst fluid or a residual/recurrent mass always means image + biopsy.
In newly diagnosed breast cancer, axillary ultrasound is the standard pre-operative test to stage the axilla. It looks for abnormal-looking lymph nodes so that nodal disease can be identified before surgery and the correct axillary operation planned — sparing node-negative patients unnecessary clearance while ensuring node-positive patients get definitive treatment. See Breast cancer ›
1What the scan is looking for
Axillary USS assesses the size and internal architecture of axillary nodes. A normal node is oval, with a thin uniform cortex and a preserved fatty hilum. Suspicious features that suggest metastatic involvement:
  • Cortical thickening >3 mm
  • Eccentric (asymmetric) cortex
  • Loss of the fatty hilum
  • Rounded rather than oval shape
  • Increased overall size
Cortex >3 mmAbsent hilumRound shape
If a node looks abnormal → USS-guided needle sampling (FNA or core biopsy) of that node.
2Sampling an abnormal node
Any suspicious node undergoes USS-guided needle biopsy. Two techniques are used:
💉FNA
Fine-needle aspiration cytology — quick, samples cells from the abnormal node.
🧬Core biopsy
Takes a tissue core — higher sensitivity, gives histology.
A positive result confirms nodal metastasis and changes the surgical plan for the axilla.
3The staging pathway — key decision logic
This is the exam-critical part. The result of axillary USS ± biopsy determines the axillary operation:
USS normal OR node biopsy NEGATIVE→Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) at time of primary surgery
USS-guided biopsy POSITIVE (proven metastasis)→Straight to axillary treatment — clearance (ANC) or radiotherapy; NO SLNB
SLNB checks for occult micrometastasis that USS cannot see. If the axilla is already proven positive, SLNB is unnecessary because definitive treatment (axillary node clearance or axillary radiotherapy) is indicated regardless. This triage spares node-negative patients the lymphoedema risk of unnecessary clearance.
🚩
A normal axillary USS does NOT exclude micrometastasis — a sentinel lymph node biopsy is still required at surgery to check for occult disease. Conversely, biopsy-proven nodal disease mandates definitive axillary treatment (clearance or radiotherapy) and the patient skips SLNB.
📷 Image placeholder — side-by-side axillary USS images: a normal oval node with a thin cortex and bright central fatty hilum, versus an abnormal rounded node with cortical thickening >3 mm and loss of the hilum, with a needle in situ for USS-guided biopsy.
🎓 Exam pearl. Learn the fork: node biopsy NEGATIVE or not done → SLNB at surgery; node biopsy POSITIVE → straight to axillary clearance/radiotherapy, no SLNB. The single most examined suspicious USS feature is cortical thickening >3 mm with loss of the fatty hilum. Never say a normal USS rules out nodal disease — it does not.
Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is the standard way to stage the axilla in early breast cancer with a clinically and ultrasound node-negative axilla. The sentinel node is the first node draining the tumour — if it is tumour-free, the rest of the axilla is very likely tumour-free too, sparing the patient a full clearance and its morbidity. See Breast cancer ›.
🎯Who
Early breast cancer, clinically + US node-NEGATIVE axilla.
🔬How
Blue dye + radioisotope localise the sentinel node.
🛡️Why
Far less morbidity than clearance — less lymphoedema.
1Indication — the node-negative axilla
SLNB is offered to patients with early (operable) breast cancer and an axilla that is node-negative on both clinical examination and ultrasound (with normal-looking nodes, or a negative US-guided biopsy). The aim is to accurately stage the axilla without removing every node.
Node-negative axilla (clinical + US)→SLNB to stage
Biopsy-proven node-POSITIVE→Straight to axillary clearance (skip SLNB)
The same sentinel-node principle is used to stage the nodal basin in melanoma.
2Technique — dye + radioisotope + gamma probe
A dual-localisation method is used for accuracy. Patent blue dye and/or a radioisotope (technetium-99m) are injected around the tumour or peri-areolar tissue; they drain to and concentrate in the sentinel node.
Blue dye (patent blue)Radioisotope (Tc-99m)Gamma probe
  • At surgery the blue and/or “hot” node(s) are identified and excised.
  • Sent for histology — sometimes assessed intra-operatively so a positive result can be acted on in the same anaesthetic.
  • Warn patients of transient blue/green discolouration of skin and urine, and rare anaphylaxis to the dye.
3Advantage — much lower morbidity
Compared with axillary lymph node clearance (ANC), SLNB removes only 1–3 nodes, so it dramatically reduces the risk of lymphoedema, shoulder stiffness and nerve injury — while still staging the axilla reliably. This is its key exam-worthy advantage.
Negative sentinel node→No further axillary surgery needed
4Managing a positive sentinel node
If the sentinel node contains metastasis, further axillary treatment is considered — axillary clearance or axillary radiotherapy (e.g. per AMAROS). In selected low-burden cases (e.g. ACOSOG Z0011-type: 1–2 positive nodes, breast-conserving surgery + whole-breast radiotherapy) further axillary surgery may be safely omitted.
ClearanceAxillary radiotherapy (AMAROS)Omit (Z0011)
🚩
A positive sentinel node is not the end — it mandates further axillary treatment (clearance or radiotherapy). And SLNB is only for the node-negative axilla: if nodes are already biopsy-proven positive pre-operatively, go straight to axillary clearance rather than SLNB.
📷 Image placeholder — intra-operative photo of a blue-stained sentinel node in the axilla being lifted with forceps, plus an inset lymphoscintigram showing radioisotope uptake (“hot” node) in the low axilla.
🎓 Exam pearl. SLNB stages the clinically and US node-negative axilla using blue dye + radioisotope (Tc-99m) and a gamma probe; its main advantage over clearance is far less lymphoedema. A positive sentinel node → clearance or radiotherapy (AMAROS), or omit in Z0011-type patients; biopsy-proven node-positive disease bypasses SLNB and goes straight to clearance.
The Nottingham Prognostic Index (NPI) estimates prognosis in operable breast cancer and helps guide adjuvant treatment. It combines three classic pathological factors: tumour size, nodal stage and histological grade. Grade itself comes from the Nottingham (modified Scarff–Bloom–Richardson, SBR) system. See Breast cancer ›
1The NPI formula
Memorise the formula — it is a classic exam favourite:
NPI = (0.2 × size in cm) + nodal stage score + grade score
The nodal stage score reflects how many axillary nodes are involved:
No nodes involved→Score 1
1–3 nodes involved→Score 2
≥4 nodes (or apical / level III)→Score 3
The grade score is simply the histological grade (1, 2 or 3), derived from the SBR system in step 2.
2SBR histological grade (3 components)
The Nottingham/SBR system scores three components, each 1–3, then sums them (total 3–9):
📊Tubule formation
How much normal glandular/tubular architecture is preserved.
📊Nuclear pleomorphism
Variation in nuclear size and shape between tumour cells.
📊Mitotic count
Number of mitoses per high-power field.
Add the three scores to get the grade:
Sum 3–5→Grade 1 (well differentiated)
Sum 6–7→Grade 2 (moderate)
Sum 8–9→Grade 3 (poorly differentiated)
3Prognostic bands
The final NPI value falls into one of three bands (approximate 5-year survival — quote as bands):
📊NPI ≤ 3.4 — Good
~85–90% 5-year survival.
📊NPI 3.41–5.4 — Moderate
~70% 5-year survival.
📊NPI > 5.4 — Poor
~50% 5-year survival.
NPI uses classic pathology (size, nodes, grade); modern MDT practice adds receptor status (ER/PR/HER2) and gene-expression assays.
🚩
A high NPI (>5.4) or a Grade 3 tumour signals poorer prognosis and a stronger case for adjuvant chemotherapy. The final decision is made at the MDT, integrating receptor status and gene-expression data.
📷 Image placeholder — worked NPI calculation example: a 2 cm tumour (0.2 × 2 = 0.4), with 2 involved nodes (score 2) and Grade 2 (score 2) giving NPI = 4.4 (moderate band), shown beside an H&E slide annotated with the three SBR components.
🎓 Exam pearl. Learn the formula verbatim: NPI = 0.2 × size (cm) + nodal score + grade score. Remember the three SBR components as tubules, pleomorphism, mitoses (each 1–3 → sum 3–9 → Grade 1/2/3), and the bands ≤3.4 good / 3.41–5.4 moderate / >5.4 poor. Higher NPI and higher grade = worse prognosis and a stronger indication for chemotherapy.
Gene-expression profiling assays measure the activity of a panel of tumour genes to estimate the risk of distant recurrence and, crucially, to predict the benefit of adding chemotherapy to endocrine therapy. They refine the very decisions that classic pathology (size, grade, nodes) alone cannot resolve, personalising treatment for ER-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer. Breast cancer ›
1What the assays measure & the key tests
Each assay quantifies mRNA expression of a defined gene panel to produce a recurrence-risk / prognostic score. The score does two jobs: it estimates the 10-year risk of distant recurrence AND — uniquely — predicts how much benefit chemotherapy would add on top of endocrine therapy. This is information staging alone does not give you.
🧬Oncotype DX
21-gene Recurrence Score (RS 0–100); the most-cited assay, validated by TAILORx.
🧬EndoPredict
12-gene score combined with tumour size and nodal status (EPclin) for a prognostic estimate.
🧬Prosigna (PAM50)
50-gene assay giving a Risk-of-Recurrence score plus intrinsic molecular subtype.
🧬MammaPrint
70-gene signature classifying tumours as low or high genomic risk (MINDACT trial).
NICE recommends these tests to guide the chemotherapy decision in the appropriate group — they complement, not replace, receptor status and staging.
2Who is eligible
Reserve these assays for the patient in whom the chemotherapy decision is genuinely uncertain — typically intermediate clinical risk on tools such as the NPI or PREDICT. The tumour must be:
Early invasiveER-positiveHER2-negativeNode-negative (or limited node+)
HER2-positive OR triple-negative→do NOT use — these have their own clear chemotherapy indications
3How the result changes management
The score converts a difficult judgement into an evidence-based decision:
LOW score→very low chemo benefit → endocrine therapy alone, sparing chemo toxicity
HIGH score→greater recurrence risk & chemo benefit → add chemotherapy to endocrine therapy
  • TAILORx (Oncotype DX) showed chemotherapy can be safely omitted in low/intermediate scores in many node-negative women.
  • The big win is de-escalation: many ER-positive patients avoid chemotherapy they would not have benefited from.
  • The result guides the MDT alongside receptor status and staging — it does not override clinical judgement.
🚩
Gene-expression profiling is NOT for HER2-positive or triple-negative disease — these already have clear chemotherapy indications and must not be denied treatment on the basis of a score never validated in them. The assay guides but does not replace MDT decision-making with receptor status and staging.
📷 Image placeholder — a decision-flow diagram: early ER+/HER2−/node-negative tumour with intermediate PREDICT risk → gene-expression assay → low score branch to endocrine therapy alone, high score branch to endocrine therapy plus chemotherapy.
🎓 Exam pearl. Gene-expression profiling (Oncotype DX, EndoPredict, Prosigna, MammaPrint) is for early ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative breast cancer to predict chemotherapy benefit: low score → endocrine therapy alone, high score → add chemotherapy. Its purpose is to spare unnecessary chemotherapy. It is not used in HER2-positive or triple-negative disease and complements — never replaces — receptor status, staging, and the MDT.
